evidence: Cic. Phil. 2.24: societātem cum aliquō coīre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A union for a common purpose (Lewis & Short): to cooperate with someone is societātem coīre cum aliquō, to share a task in societāte esse. Its other common sense is society, fellowship in general (see society-people, company-firm).

evidence: Liv. 1.17.5: rem inter sē cōnsociant (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Red. Sen. 16: cōnsilia cum aliquō cōnsociāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To make something common, to go into it together: plans, power, a task.
Rare and late, with the verb cooperārī of Christian Latin (Dominō cooperante, Vulg. Marc. 16.20); in classical prose, societās or a verb with ūnā (see together).

phrases.latin: numquam est fidēlis cum potente societās
phrases.english: a partnership with the powerful is never to be trusted

phrases.latin: dīligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum
phrases.english: for those who love God all things work together for good

sources: Lewis & Short: societas · Lewis & Short: consocio · Lewis & Short: cooperatio · Lewis & Short: cooperor
Phaedrus from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-phaedrus); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
